claims.text: A CRL is a list of revoked certificates that a CA signs and publishes at intervals; anyone can fetch it and keep a copy.
claims.source_hint: RFC 5280 §5 (CRL profile: signed by the issuer, thisUpdate/nextUpdate); glossary term crl

claims.text: With OCSP a verifier asks a responder about one certificate and gets a signed answer about its status.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6960 §2 (request for a certificate's status; responses are signed); glossary term ocsp

claims.text: A trusted timestamp is signed by a timestamp authority over a hash sent to it, binding that hash to the time the TSA makes the timestamp, from its own clock; the requester does not set that time and the TSA does not see the document.
claims.source_hint: RFC 3161 §2.1, §2.4 (TSA signs messageImprint, a hash, with genTime); glossary terms trusted-timestamp, timestamp-authority

claims.text: Payments sends the TSA only a hash, never the statement itself, so a private statement can be timestamped without handing its content to a third party.
The server's time cannot prove the signing time: whoever holds a leaked key can sign with any time the server shows, so can date a statement before a revocation.

ADR 0029: Payments signs each statement in the provider's HSM service (ADR 0023) with a key created in the HSM and used only for this bank's statements; its certificate is issued by a CA the bank names (assumed). Payments sends the HSM the statement's hash and gets the signature back.
ADR 0029: Payments gets a timestamp from a TSA over the signature, sending only a hash, not the statement; the review's diagram labels the arrow to the TSA 'hash of the signature'.
ADR 0029 takes the revocation status at signing time from the CA in one of two ways: the CA's OCSP responder first, the CA's CRL when there is no responder.
The package holds the statement's exact bytes, the signature, the certificate chain, the timestamp and the revocation status.

Every signing request, timestamp request and status fetch writes one entry to the audit log of docs/design/audit-log.md, outside Payments' tables; the bank's check does not read it; after a leak it shows which statements Payments really asked to sign.
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/0029 @ stage-4 lines 46-47; docs/team/bank-signing-requirements.md KS-5; docs/design/bank-signing-design-review.md line 104

claims.text: If the HSM, TSA or CA fails, statements wait and are retried within hours (assumed); taking orders and refunds are not affected. The TSA's certificate also ends, so packages are timestamped again before it does, as a recurring job.

The bank checks a package alone, in order: signature against the certificate's public key over the exact bytes; chain up to a root it trusts; timestamp from a TSA it trusts, giving the signing time; saved status showing the certificate valid at that time.
With the status saved at signing, the bank's check years later needs no CA service still running; the CA's services may no longer be running then.
InvoiceCertificates.cs trusts only Đơn Hàng's own root, which the bank does not trust, and its chain check sets RevocationMode to NoCheck, checking no revocation.
Stage-4 has no code that signs statements; InvoiceSigning.cs and InvoiceCertificates.cs in samples/ are unchanged.
The exact signed bytes are kept with the signature, because serialising the document again later may not give the same bytes and the signature covers only these (InvoiceSigning.cs comment).

ADR 0029's received comments: accounting asked whether all old statements must be re-signed when the certificate ends; no, the timestamp and saved status show validity at signing; only the timestamp must be renewed.
A second bank is an open review question owned by the team lead (one key per bank?), and ADR 0029 lists a second bank needing statements as a reason to revisit.

Trade-offs: server time and own root (no third party; bank trusts neither) vs TSA timestamp (one more service, re-timestamping); status at check time (smaller package, CA must still run) vs saved status (larger package, no CA call).
If the bank's CA runs no OCSP responder, Payments saves the CRL fetched at signing as the status; the bank's check does not change, but a CRL can be up to one publication interval old.

Try it: a timestamp after the revocation fails step 4 whatever date the statement states; no timestamp fails step 3; one signed before the revocation passes even if the key had leaked, and the audit log shows if Payments asked for it.
claims.source_hint: derived from docs/design/bank-signing-design-review.md @ stage-4 lines 50-56 and line 104

claims.text: ADR 0029 lists four options and picks the second; the first, the server's time and Đơn Hàng's own root, is rejected, as are the third (Đơn Hàng's own HSM) and the fourth (the shared invoice key).
